## Genetic Data

This project uses a set of newly collected genetic samples from Southern New Guinea, collected in 2019 as part of the Papuan Past project, and leverages existing samples drawn from XXX, also collected from the Papuan Past Project.

In total, we analyse a sample of 903 mitogenomes and 72 non-recombinant Y chromosomes (NRY).

### mtDNA Samples

mtDNA samples were sequenced using \[what technology?\] <!--# How was this done? Probably ask Franois-Xavier -->. Sequences are reconstructed tfrom the Revised Cambridge Reference Sequence (rCRS). See script `processing/create_reference_genomes.R` for processing details.

```{r}
if(!file.exists("processed_data/papua_n.fasta") & 
   !file.exists("processed_data/papua_m.fasta")){
  system("RScript processing/create_reference_genomes.R")  
}

```

### Linguistic Metadata

For the new samples, participants were asked a series of questions about their cultural and linguistic heritage. These questions are listed below:

> What is your gender?
>
> Where were you born?
>
> Where do you currently live?
>
> Where have you previously lived?
>
> What language(s) do you speak?
>
> What Tribe are you from?
>
> What Clan are you from?
>
> Where was your Father / Mother born?
>
> What language(s) does your Father / Mother speak
>
> What was your Father's / Mother's Tribe?
>
> What was your Father's / Mother's Clan?

For samples taken in the 2019 field visit, we also asked these additional questions:

> Where was your FF / FM / MM / MF born?
>
> What language(s) does your FF / FM / MM / MF speak?
>
> What was your FF / FM / MM / MF 's Tribe?
>
> What was your FF / FM / MM / MF 's Clan?
>
> Which hand is your dominant hand? \* related to other research questions not discussed here

From the questions on language, we also infer the language families that individuals, and relatives speak. Existing samples also contained information on the language which individuals speak. Since the braoder genetic sample was collected across a number of different studies, we make some decisions on language names, locations, and the comparability of questions across samples. See scripts `processing/add_daru.R` and `processing/format_geneticdata.R` for details on metadata cleaning and alignment.


# Building Phylogenies

## mtDNA

We have split mtDNA samples into M and N haplotype groups for computational efficiency.

<!--# might exclude the IQTree bit -->

For an initial assessment of appropriate models, we ran IQTree2 [@minh2020]. This command constructs a maximum-likelihood tree for 1000 bootstraps, testing the likelihood of XX models.

```{bash eval = FALSE}
iqtree2 -s ./processed_data/papua_m.fasta -B 1000 -T AUTO
iqtree2 -s ./processed_data/papua_n.fasta -B 1000 -T AUTO
```

These models returned the following results:

We use BEAST v2.7.4 to infer the genealogical relationships between our set of XXX mitogenomes. Here we detail the decisions behind the parameters used for our phylogenetic models, which can also be found in the .xmls file associated with this project.

### Substitution and Site model

We use a General Time Reversible (GTR) model, with a Gamma prior containing four rate categories. A GTR model assumes different rates of change between the all nucleotides, and that those rates are bi-directional (i.e. adenine (A) to guanine (G) occurs at the same rate of G to A). A Gamma prior over the rates allows for rate heterogeneity across sites, with a possibility of four rate categories. The shape parameter is estimated, with a starting value of 1 (default).

Approximately 70% of sites are invariant, so we also implement an invariant sites model, which is estimated from the data. We use empirical base frequencies for each base in this model, and all rates are estimated, except for the CT rate. At least one of the substitutions rates needs to be fixed, because estimating them all leads to model unidentifiability. We fix the transition of CT to 1 in this model, since BEAST scales rates so that the average is 1. Fixing a transition rate is more stable than fixing a transversion rate.

This model can be described as: **GTR+G4+I**

#### Clock model / Mutation Rates

We use a strict clock mutation rate, with a normal prior. Setting a normal prior on the mutation rate means we accommodate uncertainty in the tree-wide rate, but rates do no vary across branches, as is standard with a strict clock.

We determine mtDNA mutations rates from studies calibrating the human mitochondrial clock (@rieux2014, @fu2013). In both studies we consider the whole genome substitution rate. We take the mean mutation rate from both papers to be the mean of the normal prior, and the lowest and highest rates in the range to be the upper and lower values of the distribution.

|             Paper | Estimated Mean Mutation Rate |  Estimated 95% C.I.   |
|------------------:|:----------------------------:|:---------------------:|
|    Fu et al. 2013 |        2.67 x 10^-8^         | 2.16 - 3.16 x 10^-8^  |
| Rieux et al. 2014 |        2.143 x 10^-8^        | 1.58 - 2.706 x 10^-8^ |
|         Used here |       2.4065 x 10^-8^        | 1.58 - 3.16 x 10^-8^  |

### Tree Prior

We use a Coalescent Extended Bayesian Skyline Population history model (EBSP). The EBSP model leverages coalescent theory to account for fluctuating population size in the phylogenetic model, at multiple loci (Heled & Drummond, 2008). The sparsity of historical knowledge in Southern New Guinea means we do not have a good understanding of changes in population size. We opt for using a model that will allow for a fluctuating population, rather than assuming that it did not fluctuate.

### MCMC Settings

We run the tree for 10,000,000 iterations, storing every 10,000 iterations.

# Trait Heritage

To estimate the fidelity of language transmission over time, we calculate the probability of two individuals sharing a language within a genetic clade, across multiple times point in the phylogenetic history. This calculation follow from [@lansing2017].

$$
P(i_l,j_l)|i_{g(t)}, j_{g(t)}) = \frac{P(i_l, j_l \bigcap i_{g(t)}, j_{g(t)})}{P(i_{g(t)}, j_{g(t)}} = \frac{\sum_{g=1}^{c_t}(\sum_{i,j\neq i}1_{cos(l_ig, l_jg) > 0})}{\sum_{g=1}^{c_t}n_g(n_g - 1) / 2}
$$

$c_t$ is the number of genetic clades at any point in history, for t generations. We assume 25 year generation times. $l_{i_g}$ and $l_{j_g}$ are the languages or language families spoken by individuals within genetic clade $g$. $1_{cos(l_{i_g}, l_{i_g}) > 0}$ is 1 if the ith and jth individual share a language, and zero otherwise. $n_g$ is the number of individuals in $g$.

We calculate the trait heritage for a number of different traits.

-   Language of individual

-   Language family of individual

-   Language of individual's father's father

-   Language of individual's mother's mother

-   Language family of individual's father's father

-   Language family of individual's mother's mother

We extend this calculation to calculate the probability of a trait given a further conditions

-   The shared language is a Trans-New Guinea language

-   The shared language is not a Trans-New Guinea language

As with [@lansing2017], we compare the calculated probability with a permuted probability to determine whether languages are more likely to be shared by chance. We calculate XXX permutations per analysis.

We apply the trait heritage function across a posterior of trees. Within each tree we calculate the probability from the data, and the XXX permutations.

The trait heritage functions have been collected into a package that can be found here: <https://github.com/SamPassmore/traitheritage>

#### Average marriage distance

```{r}
village_location = read.csv("data/metadata_villagedata.csv") %>% 
  select(village, Latitude, Longitude) %>% 
  distinct(village, .keep_all = TRUE) %>% 
  filter(village != "" & !is.na(village) & !is.na(Latitude))

village_distance = distm(village_location[, c("Longitude", "Latitude")], fun = distHaversine)
dimnames(village_distance) = list(village_location$village, village_location$village)

fathers_village = metadata$father_village[metadata$father_village %in% rownames(village_distance)]
mothers_village = metadata$mother_village[metadata$mother_village %in% rownames(village_distance)]

parents_dist = c()
for(i in 1:nrow(metadata)){
  fv = metadata$father_village[i]
  mv = metadata$mother_village[i]
  
  if(fv %in% rownames(village_distance) & mv %in% rownames(village_distance)){
    parents_dist[i] = village_distance[fv, mv]  
  }
  
}


```

#### mtDNA Trait heritage

```{r echo=FALSE}
mcct_tree = read.nexus("NCI/mtDNA_N/mtDNA_N-papua_n_daru.mcct.trees")

language_probability = 
  read.csv("results/interview_languagefamily_mtDNA_N-papua_n_daru_languagefamily.csv")

permuted_probability = 
  read.csv("results/interview_languagefamily_mtDNA_N-papua_n_daru_permuted_languagefamily.csv")

summarizer = function(posterior){
  posterior$generation_time = as.numeric(gsub("g_", replacement = "", posterior$generation))
  posterior %>%
  filter(!is.na(clade_probability)) %>% # remove NA clades. Usually occur because of singleton clades
  group_by(generation_time) %>%
  summarise(mean.prob = mean(clade_probability, na.rm = TRUE),
            ci_hdi = bayestestR::ci(clade_probability), # 95% credible interval
            n_matches = sum(numerator_sum)) %>% 
  tidyr::unpack(ci_hdi)
}

# Summarise the posterior
posterior_summary = summarizer(language_probability)
permuted_summary = summarizer(permuted_probability )

cleaned_tips = gsub("_.*","", mcct_tree$tip.label)
mcct_tree$tip.label = cleaned_tips

metadata_ss = metadata[metadata$ID %in% mcct_tree$tip.label, ]
mcct_tree = keep.tip(mcct_tree, metadata_ss$ID[!is.na(metadata_ss$interview_languagefamily)])

tree_data = full_join(mcct_tree, metadata, by = c("label" = "ID"))

#### plot 
p_tree = ggtree(tree_data) + geom_tippoint(aes(color = daru)) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = c(10000, 20000, 30000, 40000),
                     labels = c("10k", "20k", "30k", "40k")) +
  layout_dendrogram() + 
  theme(legend.position = "none", 
        axis.ticks.y = element_line(),
        axis.line.y = element_line(),
        axis.text.y = element_text())

# match scales in each plot
x_range = layer_scales(p_tree)$x$range$range
  
p_prob = ggplot(data = posterior_summary,
                aes(ymin = CI_low, ymax = CI_high, x = generation_time, y = mean.prob)) +
  geom_ribbon(fill = "lightblue", alpha = 0.5) + 
  geom_line(col = "blue") + 
  geom_ribbon(data = permuted_summary, 
              aes(ymin = CI_low, ymax = CI_high, x = generation_time, y = mean.prob),
              fill = "lightgreen", alpha = 0.5) + 
  geom_line(data = permuted_summary, 
              aes(x = generation_time, y = mean.prob),
            col = "forestgreen") + 
  ylim(c(0, 1)) +
  xlim(x_range) + ## max tree height (or max p_tree?)
  coord_flip() +
  xlab("") + 
  ylab("") + 
  # scale_x_continuous(expand = c(0, 0)) + 
  # scale_y_continuous(expand = c(0, 0)) + 
  theme_classic() + 
  theme(panel.grid.major = element_blank(), 
        panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
        panel.background = element_rect(colour = "black", linewidth=0.5))

p_tree + p_prob + 
  plot_layout(widths = c(1, 0.25))

```

These next graphs show the probability of shared language family against geographic proximity. we test geographic proximity at three distances: are two individuals within 50km of each other, 100kms, or 200kms.

```{r}
distance50_probability = read.csv("results/interview_languagefamily_mtDNA_N-papua_n_daru_distance50.csv")
distance100_probability = read.csv("results/interview_languagefamily_mtDNA_N-papua_n_daru_distance100.csv")
distance200_probability = read.csv("results/interview_languagefamily_mtDNA_N-papua_n_daru_distance200.csv")

distance_summary = lapply(list(short = distance50_probability,
                        medium = distance100_probability,
                        long = distance200_probability), 
                        summarizer)

distance_summary = bind_rows(distance_summary, .id = "distance")
distance_summary$distance = factor(distance_summary$distance, 
                                   levels = c("short", "medium", "long"))

facet_names = c(`short` = "w/n 50km",
                `medium` = "w/n 100km",
                `long` = "w/n 200km")

ggplot(data = distance_summary,
       aes(
         ymin = CI_low,
         ymax = CI_high,
         x = generation_time,
         y = mean.prob
       )) +
  geom_ribbon(fill = "lightgreen", alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_line(data = distance_summary,
            aes(x = generation_time, y = mean.prob),
            col = "forestgreen") +
  facet_grid(~ distance, labeller = as_labeller(facet_names)) +
  geom_ribbon(
    data = posterior_summary,
    aes(
      ymin = CI_low,
      ymax = CI_high,
      x = generation_time,
      y = mean.prob
    ),
    fill = "lightblue",
    alpha = 0.5
  ) + geom_line(data = posterior_summary,
                aes(x = generation_time,
                    y = mean.prob),
                col = "blue") +
  scale_x_reverse(breaks = c(0, 10000, 20000, 30000, 40000, 50000),
                  labels = c("0", "10k", "20k", "30k", "40k", "50k")) + 
  xlab("Time (years)") + 
  ylab("Probability") + 
  theme_classic()
  

```

```{r}
  xlab("Time (years)") + 
  ylab("Probability") + 
  theme_classic()

```
